One day, a few years ago, my mother suddenly handed me an online IQ test and I immediately started solving it. Since that day, there was a place in my mind reserved for the number 136. I used to think I need to be perfect to be valuable. No one told me that this way, this is just how I felt. But gladly, I already learned that it's not true.

I have a request for a topic. I've often thought of myself as resilient, but lately I'm starting to understand it's more like functioning through extreme avoidance. Not resilience, but barely hanging on for years at a time by pushing everything to the side.

I've also discovered that dissociation disorders are a wide range. I always thought DID was the movie-style persona switching. Apparent;y not. Apparently most cases are more like occasional backseat drivers and severe memory issues, something subtle and hidden.

And that's my topic request. I suffer from pretty severe memory issues. I know the causes could be anything from abuse, the physical damage, to surviving difficult situations, and more. It seems like the brain had a knack for saying "this cluster of neurons is too much to handle right now, so let's just put a little wall up and function as if they aren't there.". (Honestly, I suspect that's the cause of the movie-style DID, but that's a different topic.)

I was thinking of a dive into memory issues, their causes, their effects, and how living with them feels. Especially the phenomenon of the brain hiding the memory gaps. Amnesia of the amnesia, or something. You don't even realize you're forgetting things until someone points it out or it because a noticeable problem. Like how you can watch a movie one day, and forget you watched it during a conversation with someone the next day. And suddenly they say something that triggers the network of connections in your mind and you do remember watching it, embarrassed and confused as to how you could have forgotten.

Honestly, people think you're lying half the time too. They don't understand not being able to access your own knowledge and memory pathways normally, and assume people are making up weird lies for no reason. 

Those little cells going "nuh uh, I'm blocking this painful signal." create so much havoc on the larger memory structure. I wouldn't be surprised if most people have some small form of dissociation and never notice it.

i am turning 19 in a month.

i have depression since age 12, later got diagnosed with an anxiety neurosis at around age 15-16.

not only that, but ive got neurologically diagnosed with "underdeveloped nervous system" due to the damage the prolonged stress and trauma since age 5 brought with itself.

in the same year, ive randomly dissociated while on a trip with my parents and ex-bf.
i left the car to admire the sightings around me, but as i looked around, the world slowly began to feel unreal, detaching me completely from it.

its been 3 years since that.
i have ZERO access to my emotions, my brain is foggy af, i have no sense of time and lost all my reflex.
sometimes it gets so bad to the point where i hv to pinch myself or hold my hands under cold water to evoke strong stimulus — which grounds me bk.

bcz of that fuckass derealization-depersonalization, i CANNOT get a driving license.
had 3 attempts, failed each one of them... evb tells me im a good driver, but bcz im not "there" mentally, i cannot react to things quickly...
thats also the reason why i was so anxious each time i had my driving lessons and had to sit behind the wheel.
i put ALL the effort i could to be in touch w the world and act in real-time.
after the lessons i often got headaches from the insane focus it required.

i was supposed to get the license before summer break started on 26th june... it didnt work the first time and the next two times too.
the license would easen up my life a lot — i could finally find a summer job, bcz i live in a small fucking isolated village (22kms to the closest urban area) and drive myself comfortably to the city my boarding school is located in (77km away).

i feel sick js at the thought of returning bk to school on 1st sep, and having to endure extreme stress each morning, bcz i cant get ready in time, and i only hv one bus.
no matter how early i wake up, my movements are too slow that even 2 hrs is sometimes not enough to js dress up, wash my face, brush my teeth and hair then do makeup — i dont even hv time to eat. i get a quick snack when i arrive to the city hours later.
my parents get extremely annoyed when i miss the bus, and my dad has to wake up way earlier to drive me to the bus station in that town 22kms away (hes going to work later).

not to mention that my school is located high, and i hv to go uphill which results in burning lungs and heart aching from the exhaustion.
i hv rlly poor lung capacity, even though my legs move fast.
it takes me around 15 mins to walk from the bus station to the school.

caffeine is mandatory in my life, without it i feel like some mf vegetable or a zombie. not only physically but mentally too.

i asked my mom to sign me up for the EMDR therapy which is specific for dissociation treatment.
unfortunately finding any professional help in my area is RLLY difficult and expensive.
i rlly hope it works out, bcz i cant get the mf license if i dont snap out of the 3-year long dissociation beforehand...

i learned to live with my depression and anxiety, but the dissociation is something that SRSLY influences and worsens ur daily functioning.
i got used to it and thought its bearable, until it proved me wrong when i kept on failing the practical driving exam...

i am under constant support of a psychiatrist, still being medicated to this day, but we are trying to get me off meds.
rn, its js some mood stabilizers and dopamine.
through the 7 years, i was on very diff medication bcz nothing worked.
had my psychiatrist changed once too, around 2-3 yrs ago, idk.

i hv to force myself to live and function on the daily, with my parents being the only reason im still there.
i promised to stay strong for em, as they were the only ppl (and my close family kinda too) to be by my side and support me since i went to that fuckass hell-on-earth kindergarten.
society destroyed me, not js some silly bullying from the kids but degrading treatment from the adults too (teachers, workers, etc.)

i dont need pity, js wanted to share some of my personal experience and hope that there are atleast a few people out there who actually understand and can sympathize — maybe even find some similarities and can relate :)

Ingredients
​Bread: 2 thick slices of sourdough or brioche 
​Cheese: \frac{1}{2} cup shredded sharp cheddar + \frac{1}{2} cup shredded gruyère (or low-moisture mozzarella)
​Spread: 1 tbsp room-temperature butter + 1 tbsp mayonnaise
​Flavor Boost: \frac{1}{8} tsp garlic powder + pinch of flaky sea salt
​Instructions
​Prep the Crunch Paste: Mix the softened butter, mayonnaise, and garlic powder in a small bowl. Spread this mixture evenly on one side of each bread slice. (The mayo raises the smoke point and creates an extra crisp crust). 
​Build the Sandwich: Flip the slices over so the buttered sides are facing down. Pile the cheese blend evenly onto one slice, then cap it with the second slice (buttered-side up).
​Low & Slow Sear: Heat a skillet over medium-low heat. Place the sandwich in the pan and cover with a lid for 3–4 minutes to help the cheese melt without burning the bread.
​Flip & Toast: Remove the lid, flip carefully, and cook the other side uncovered for another 3–4 minutes until deep golden brown and crispy.
​Finish: Sprinkle a pinch of flaky sea salt on top, slice diagonally, and enjoy immediately!

*Key Points to Remember After You Watch The Video. (Thank Me Later):*
1. Your brain has a special part called the fusiform gyrus that acts like a filing cabinet to help you recognize and store faces (0:53-1:00).

2. Most faces look average, so your brain files them away quickly to save energy, which is why you forget them easily (1:03-1:17).

3. You are more likely to remember someone if they have a unique feature, like bright hair or a scar, because your brain pauses to create a detailed file for them (1:20-1:36).

4. If you feel like you have met someone before or have an instant connection, your brain might be matching their face or voice to a memory of someone else you already know (3:12-3:33).

5. Some people have face blindness, which means their brain does not process faces correctly, so they use other clues like voice, clothes, or hair to tell people apart (3:46-4:18).

6. To help yourself remember faces, pick one unique feature to focus on, ask questions to learn more about the person, or practice mentally drawing them right after you meet (5:00-6:08).

comment_text:
As someone who knows others with ADHD but myself think I only have the HSP trait, I can say I've found some differences in how our brains work. 

We share a lot in common but like the video said, they seem to come from different things or work differently to produce the same outcome. 

The biggest example I can think of is mental focus. My friend who has ADHD doesn't focus well when their brain is dealing with something they don't like or have any interest in, but can be really focused on topics they are. For myself, I can focus on pretty much anything if I make myself interested in it. Which is something I've noticed ADHD people have a harder time doing. 

A realistic example is that my friend with ADHD used to get really behind on schoolwork because he procrastinated. A result of his executive function not working as well because he wasn't stimulated enough by the work. (Even if he wanted to, he struggled) 

For me, I saw schoolwork as a task to be done even if I wasn't interested in it, so I made myself sit down and work on it. This task was easier for me to start, but once I got into it, I was really focused on it. To the point I worked on a paper for 5 hours straight, forgot to eat my food I made beforehand, and the next day I felt like I blacked out because I was so focused. I called it hyperfocus. (I often forget to eat because of it)

I get overwhelmed by my emotions a lot. I had a nightmare once that when I woke up, even though it wasn't actually that bad, it triggered my anxiety to the point I started uncontrollably crying. I always thought it was my anxiety, but I feel like my emotions cause my anxiety instead of the other way around because my worst moments are always with emotional overwhelm or mental exhaustion. Which happens very easily for me. I need a lot of alone time to recover. I even get teary eyed just by having some kind of emotional connection with someone in a conversation when I don't even know them. The conversation can be something simple like what makes them happy. (I definitely know I'm an empathetic cryer)

I have sensory issues as well but they work both in good and bad ways. The sound of eating can make me irrationally angry. Yet everything being the same color in a room relaxes my mind and makes me feel a sense of euphoria. I used to think it was related to OCD, but I don't get compulsions. I just get happier with some sensations, and I get really bothered by others. 

It's something that effects all 5 of my senses. 

Just something I thought to share.

I see the overlap of HSP and neurodivergence the same way as hEDS (Hypermobile Elhers-Danlos Syndrome) and HSD (Hypermobile Spectrum Disorder) operate.

Both hEDS and HSD have hypermobility stemming from collagen makeup differences and can cause real-life difficulties with chronic pain, but if a person doesn’t fulfill the requirements for a hEDS diagnosis, they are diagnosed with HSD.

The same can be said with ASD/ADHD and being a HSP. One may not fulfill all of the diagnostic requirements needed for a formal diagnosis of ASD or ADHD, but they still have many of the traits of either or both, which still gives them trouble in their day-to-day life, and therefore still having a different lived experience than the average neurotypical person. I see HSP as a sort of middle ground, "neurodivergent-light" if you will😅

I am going to high school right now, and in all of the time I've been in it (I am a senior now), I've only cried... one time.





It was during my Modern U.S. History class. We were watching this documentary on the Vietnam War to finish off our unit over the war. The ending concluded with it explaining the black scar with the names of the Vietnam war engraved into it. It was as I thought about this some more as the college student who designed the scar explained it in the documentary that I began breaking out in tears. My closest friend is an immigrant from Vietnam, and I'm highly empathetic due to my ASD. I guess both of these things plus everything else I had bottled up combined to cause me to cry uncontrollably for the next 15 minutes. Even and everyone left for lunch (I held up my teacher since be couldn't leave until I did), my friend from Vietnam stayed and tried to help by saying I shouldn't cry for him. It wasn't just for him. I'm 22. I used to seek help at the college's therapist to fix my chronic overthinking but turns out that it is useless. I am now paying for  structured Cognitive Behaviour Therapy sessions and I learnt 2 main things: 'Reframing' thoughts and 'Acceptance'. But we are given a rare ability to relate to people more and a larger capacity to be kind. Of course, everyone's brain is wired differently and my suggestions might not work for everyone.

I am reading Fyodor Dostoevsky's works, and its an activity I would do to make me feel better, because he explores the depth of human psyche through the characters and the author's understanding genuinely makes me feel that I'm not alone. comment_text:
Best step to take without a doubt:

Getting to know yourself beyond your trauma.

You have to love someone in the present. Trauma is about the past.

If you only know about your trauma, you only know about a part of you. Despite it meaning a lot and affecting you significantly, you're still someone with things you like, things you seek, things that make you feel comfortable ... etc.

You're still someone with social habits, motivators, motivations, stressors, etc. That go beyond whatever has happened to you in the past.

Find those things, little by little, and you will start feeling like you can escape this spiral of despair that only knowing your traumatised self is.

For example - I am a physically passive, but psychologically very active friend. I can heed words, maybe not memorise them, but can also lend aid when a problem exists. I'm someone who likes cars, loves to draw and paint, and loves animals as well. I'm thinking I might also love the idea of sculpting, and pretty much everything else that has to do with art.
     I'm very live let live, and also very compassionate. I can forgive many things - to a fault, really.
      My favourite colour is white, and I really like music. A lot.

Edit:

Please, know that this step is reserved only once you understand where your traumatised self resides. You cannot ignore it either, as it is still a part of you - you just can eventually stop depending on it.


People tend to make the mistake of trying to make something work when all they have is pain - and a relationship that works only by sharing pain is most often gonna stay painful.

In real life zen masters are not necessarily calm, actually some of them were incredibly anxious or angry (and enlightened, you can check Hakuin or Sojun), and there are other awakened characters like U G Krishnamurti famous for being bitter and rude.

Calm people tend to be incredibly immature: you have a conflict with them and they simply repress their feelings and they cannot react. You want to know if someone is emotionally mature? You tell them when they hurt you "You've hurt me". If they get defensive, they withdraw, they cannot give you an apology with the four elements of an apology, they cannot take accountability, that's it, they're immature. Overthinking is treated here as a cognitive habit, something happening inside the individual that the individual can learn to manage. And that's true. But there's a layer underneath it worth looking at.
A lot of the overthinking people experience - especially the social kind, the "what did they mean by that message" kind - isn't just anxiety finding a target. It's a predictable response to communication environments that were specifically designed to produce ambiguity. Read receipts that show someone saw your message but didn't reply. Reactions that replace words. Texts stripped of tone, facial expression, timing, everything that would have resolved the uncertainty in seconds if the conversation had happened face to face.
The overthinking spiral isn't a glitch in that system. It's closer to a feature. A person stuck in a rumination loop keeps checking. Keeps re-reading. Keeps engaging. The architecture benefits from the uncertainty it creates.
Which doesn't make the framework less useful - it makes it more necessary. But it does add a question worth paying attention to: how much of what feels like your anxiety is actually a designed stimulus that found you?

Hey everyone, we wanted to talk openly for a moment.

Over the last 8 years, Psych2Go has tried to build more than just a YouTube channel. We wanted this to feel like a safe corner of the internet. A place where people could admit they were struggling, cry if they needed to, ask questions they were too scared to ask elsewhere, or simply feel less alone for a few minutes.

So we wanted to ask you directly:

What do you think is the best course of action for protecting a mental health community online while still staying true to compassion and openness?

comment_text:
I appreciate the message :)
I double appreciate the maturity of pointing out that the people who are being "mean" are not necessarily bad people. It's really easy in modern society to have being "mean" be the way that you learn to be social at all. A lot of people struggle to communicate what they're feeling because the only thing they've been surrounded by is veiled insults, sarcasm, grandstanding, or something else similar.
Even if they don't like how it lands, it may be the only words/phrasing that they can come up with.

Some may learn that easily and adjust, others may only learn the hard way. I was fortunate early on to learn the hard way, but not so badly that it steered me away from being social entirely. With that in mind, not everyone deserves your kindness. The previous me that was being mean for no reason, didn't deserve to be treated gently, and its because someone finally was mean back to me, that it made me uncomfortable. Uncomfortable because I was being confronted that *I* was in charge of my words. That I could choose another way to come across.

It's not an instant shift into being a better person, but it starts the process of learning how to communicate in different ways so that you can actually try and adapt what you say to reflect how you feel. 
Again, the point is that not everyone deserves your kindness. No one (socially) enjoys your mean-ness. Use them both when they're appropriate though. Confronting someone isn't always JUST mean, some times its a way of caring, or of guidance if you actually hint at them how you could see them improving. Kindness applied in a blanket fashion doesn't always feel good either, use it tastefully so that it always means something when you say it. Be a whole person, and not just part of one.

Ohh, since we were invited to share, well.. I don't think it's even possible to completely get rid of overthinking. Only today (funny coincidence) I was trying to figure out why I do that so much, especially at most inconvenient and intimate moments... And I actually did find out something!! It's deeply rooted in my social anxiety and threat detecting mechanisms. For example, the so called "social instinct" (which is extremely developed in me, it might even be genetic since my mother and my maternal cousin both have that too), it makes me think a lot about people that my close ones have judged and my brain very masterfully links the unwanted behaviour of such people.. to my own. I might not even be like them, but my brain is very convinced I am, as it's probably trying to have me never repeat the despised behaviour, so I don't get "kicked out of the tribe", haha... The same thing is when I talk, basically to anyone. At the moment of communication I can't truly process anything, sometimes I even manage to speak coherently somehow, which is a surprise... But after the moment is over, I replay every small detail I did, every little subtle expression of my conversationalist and.. usually it leads me to the thought that I failed. And some moments that were most humiliating to me (for other people it usually was just a conversation and nothing more) might stick to me for years. 
If it would be helpful to know, I was diagnosed with social anxiety and BPD by a psychiatrist, and I also sometimes have inconsistent OCD patterned behaviours...
As for how I manage it, well.. I'm not always able to. But when I am, like today, I usually try to dissociate from those intrusive thoughts... Today I've learned something meaningful: the taboo intrusive thoughts that come to me does not mean I secretly desire the things that come up to my mind, it just means that my brain, prone to analysis and association thinking, is trying to protect me from things it thinks I shouldn't do to stay a "good" person and be safe...
I don't know if you'll read it, but I hope this was helpful!! (⁠ ⁠；⁠∀⁠；⁠)

The impulse to remove people isn't primarily a character choice shaped by pop psychology - it's a regulatory behavior. What looks like intolerance is often a nervous system running threat-response. It's what's driving the impulse in the first place, and whether the capacity for the more sophisticated response is actually there yet.

Oh, wow... This is a big one.
I was unsure at first whether to even watch this video or not, because "I know what my purpose is, right?", but this feeling of questioning why I'm doing all this is still so familiar. I don't wake up during the night, but it comes during the day. Over and over again. And for some reason, the solution I reach is always 'ending it all', but even that leads to another paradox, because I still chose to stay in this world (then why...?).
I major in math (2nd year) and it's draining all my energy and wants more and I still struggle (it's THAT hard). I told everyone, including myself, that I started out of passion, to become a mathematician and discover things, but that was half a lie, there was pressure involved (which is a story of its own) and I have no idea how I survive that and what I do after that. I also isolate myself most of the time, because that what I know how to do, so I don't really have a connection with anyone in my university. And it barely even leaves me time to go to the Beyblade tournaments I like so much and meet the people I actually know how to connect with. And to top it all of with "Why am I even doing all this?" makes me feel like my head is about to crack in half. Because what if I just wasted my time and energy for nothing? And what else could I do?!

This escalated much more than I thought it would. It always happens when I try to write while feeling like this. My story seems like a successful one to others, but from the inside it's such a mess. And I'm not sure if it matters for now, but having autism doesn't help that at all.

comment_text:
This is *such* an important video. I was diagnosed with OCD (along with several other neurodivergent conditions) in 2016 at the age of 42. I *do not* keep my house neat & tidy, constantly wash my hands, or wipe every surface in public places - that's not the form it takes for many people living with OCD. I can obsess about details, but they're *not* to do with germophobia - I can be "unsettled" by things like curtains not hanging straight, but can leave my kitchen worktops covered in crumbs. In fact, I'm at the opposite end of the spectrum - I am a recovering hoarder, because I find it difficult to throw *anything* away. There are 2 reasons for this: what if I/someone else can use the item, & the environmental guilt. (For anyone reading this in the UK of a certain age you'll get the reference if I say I'm a natural Womble! 😅)

However, the most debilitating thing about OCD for me is the intrusive thoughts, & the replaying over every minute detail of life, as described in this video. I have not had any therapy for my OCD, but I'm increasingly aware that I would benefit greatly from it - especially as I'm also living with AuDHD, anxiety & depression. I was also diagnosed as BPD, but given how calm I am these days, that could be a misdiagnosis, based on the frustration I *used* to expereince from being a misunderstood, undiagnosed neurodivergent. Unfortunately, mental health services have been closed down *entirely* in the area where I live, due to lack of funding going into the NHS here in the UK. Just was guided to your channel at just the right time. Thank you Jesus.

My life has been a living hell with brief moments of happiness just tolerable enough to not fully go through with "tapping out". At this day and age, probably everyone has.

One thing I learned is there are two kinds of stressors. Light attacks, and heavy attacks. Heavy attacks are like that point when something serious happens, and it just shakes your very core beliefs and identity. The one event is traumatic, and this is the type typically thought of with "Trauma"

Then there's the light attacks. These are subtle, often not even felt. They come from "I hate how I look in the mirror." to "You aren't working fast enough." To the same songs on the work radio for an 8 hour shift 30 hours a week.

The light attacks are a slow, rusty saw, cutting through your pain tolerances, then your patiences, and then your very soul.

Like Halo, when the shield goes down, you gotta take cover or you're taking health damage. But the shield has a recharge delay.  You gotta stay in cover and take no damage for a certain time for the shield to recharge.

Each of us have different shield HP, different recharge rates, and different recharge delays.

When your traumatized partner retreats to be isolated, they're taking cover and letting the shield recharge. comment_text: Something I've learned but never see talked about is my personal experience: The idea that going through something traumatizing doesn't always make you a hardened warrior. Take Katniss and Peeta from the Hunger Games. Katniss turns into that hardened warrior, while Peeta stays much softer. Sometimes you cry easier, sometimes you retreat and close off and avoid confrontation like the plague.  Sometimes they get far more scared of the world around them, and sometimes even more scared of the people around them. In what way depends on what they went through, but fear and anxiety might be at the console most of the time to also reference Inside Out. Sometimes it's not Anger or Joy or even Sadness. Trauma looks different in everybody, and for me a lot of the time what I need is a lot more comfort and reassurance than anything else. It can be hard to read or pick up on what a traumatized individual needs day to day, even hour to hour (my ptsd flashback episodes are often different almost every single time, and what helped me last time might trigger me more next time.) But being there and being ready to support them is what means the world. If they're okay talking about what helps them, have that conversation. Having someone who cares enough to actually listen means more than words can say. If you say you're there for them, Prove It. Of course if it's too much, take care of yourself. I never reach out during flashback episodes because I'm fully aware of how intense and scary they are to witness, and I don't want to put anyone through them, (backwards thinking I know, but still applicable.) Take care of yourself, you cannot pour from an empty cup. If you need space, take it. Reassure that it's just so you can recharge and that they didn't do anything wrong (if they actually didn't) and say you just need some time to recoup. Everyone is different. Take care of yourself and be there for your partner/friend/family member. Having someone who cares and the proves that they care is something we need more than anything. I'm still looking for that person, and I hope they're out there. You will find yours.

Loving someone with a difficult or resilient past does indeed mean being patient and understanding, but also accepting that sometimes there are going to be improvements in your relationship, yet they can all of a sudden turn back into what you tried to fix. So not losing sight of yourself in the process is hard. Sometimes, you can accept someone’s mistakes and still realize that the relationship is starting to take more from you than it gives. If you focus only on their history, you might end up ignoring your own needs, boundaries, and emotional limits.
And while people can change, growth doesn’t happen just because someone is cared for deeply—it has to come from them too. They must want to change for themselves; it is not for you to fix them, because that was never your job. At some point, you have to be honest with yourself about whether things are actually moving forward or whether you’re holding onto hope while your own well-being slowly erodes with every repeating choice they make. Choosing yourself doesn’t cancel out empathy; it just means you’re acknowledging that love alone isn’t always enough for change to happen, and that even if they are having a hard time, they should still be able to say to you: “You’re not alone, I just need time.”
And if they disappear when hard times come, trust me—if you explain your hurt twice, they will do it again and again. Your loved one is not the only person in the relationship who needs reassurance. You are not bad for wanting affection as well.

2 things.

- Love is complicated, and takes many different forms throughout our lives.  
We focus a lot on romantic love (I'll get to that), but there's also love in family, in friendships, in the good hearted neighbor, in the simple kindness of a stranger.  So the idea of "Was I ever really loved?" really takes on a different context when looking at love through these different lenses.  It becomes more of "what feels missing", rather than "was I ever", kind of situation.

- On the subject of romantic love; there is a parallel question/feeling involved with this is "Did they ever love me in the first place?"  This is one of those times where it's really easy to cherry pick moments to reach a conclusion, but much harder when you start looking at everything, and bring up more questions like "Is this genuine or are they wanting something?"  Someone can bombard you with gifts and you wonder if this love bombing comes from a genuine place, or if it's just a form of appeasement after a fight.  I'm sure there's a bunch more connected with this idea, but I'm sure you can come up with your own situations.

This is the Zeigarnik Effect in its purest form. Your brain prioritizes 
UNFINISHED situations—and because the conversation doesn't have closure 
(no resolution, no understanding), your brain keeps it in active memory, 
looping it endlessly.

But here's what most people miss: The more you replay it, the MORE 
unfinished it becomes, because every replay slightly rewrites the memory 
through a process called memory reconsolidation. So each replay reinforces 
it rather than solves it.

The neuroscience explains why "just stop thinking about it" doesn't work—
your brain is literally trying to solve an unsolvable puzzle. The solution 
isn't to suppress the replay; it's to update your narrative about what 
the conversation MEANS.

Once your brain classifies it as "understood and resolved" (even if nothing 
actually changed), the replay loop loses power.

This is exactly what happens psychologically—great breakdown of the mechanism.

I was unable to find anything good in that relationship, so I finally changed my prayer. Instead of asking God (however you choose to call that entity) what the good in the situation was, I asked, "Can't you find another way?" 

The next day, the narcissist said that he thought we should break up. He was trying to manipulate me, but I responded with the only words that would have worked: "You're probably right." 

Now that it's over, I am able to extract good out of that relationship. There's always something, even if we can't see it from certain angles.

Many/most people know of the recommendation of getting eight hours of sleep every night. However, what is not known is how this recommendation came about. The recommendation did not come from medical research of sleep or anything like that. Instead, during the period of the industrial revolution when the powers that be were trying to figure out the best balance for how many hours of the day a person should have to work, versus personal time, versus sleep time, it was decided to simply divide the 24 hour day into three separate segments: eight hours of work, eight hours personal time, and eight hours of sleep.
Personally, from my own research, as well as repeated, conscious trial, since the body/mind goes through these 90 minute phases which alternate from shallow sleep, which is easier for a person to wake up from, to deep sleep, which is much more difficult for a person to wake up from, typically resulting in the person being extremely groggy and disoriented, I have found that if I need to wake up at a certain time, I time my sleeping hours, from going to sleep to having to wake up, in three hour increments (3, 6, 9, etc.) I have found this practice to be the most effective way to be able to wake up when I need to with minimal effort or negative effects (grogginess, disorientation, etc.) The eight hour suggestion is typical to result in a person having to (try to) wake up near when the person is in their deepest sleep cycle(s) which naturally makes it harder to wake up, additionally the person will have the feeling of not having had enough sleep due to the resulting grogginess, (it's also why people tend to hit that snooze button so many times, i.e., the body is still trying to climb out of deep sleep.)

comment_text: Hello! I've been watching Psych2Go for a while now. Around a year and a half ago, I starting having intense panic attacks. I genuinely felt like I was going to die. Soon after I started taking medicine the help make the anxiety easier to deal with, I started becoming hyper-aware of everything that could potentially harm or kill me. And even worse, it was accompanied by these urge-like feelings that made me worry I might lose control and try to hurt or kill myself, even though I love life, I'm absolutely terrified of death and I don't want to leave my family and other loved ones behind. There were days where I was scared to step outside the house because I was convinced that something bad would happen if I did. I also sometimes just profusely cried in my bedroom over it. And I'm not exactly a crybaby, though I can be sensitive at times. I worry sometimes that my life is without worth and that unless I can answer the big, existential questions of the universe, I'll lose my will to live. Of course, I understand now that this just my brain going into survival mode. It's designed to me safe and alive, not to hurt and/or kill me. It just does too well at keeping me safe sometimes. And now that I understand that and have educated myself further on the topic, I definitely feel way better and more able to enjoy my life and be present again. To anyone else dealing with similar problems, I have this to say. Your brain is not your enemy. It's not conspiring to destroy you. It just goes to extremes to protect what matters sometimes. Try to resist the urge to argue with anxiety. Arguing with anxiety, at least for me, just makes it argue back even harder. And do try to face your fears too. It might be extremely uncomfortable at first, but it will eventually break the pattern your brain learned or at least make it easier to cope with. Just remember that your brain is ultimately your friend, even when it feels like it will betray you. And you definitely rebuild trust in yourself again. I still have crappy days sometimes, but the good days have recently been outweighing them. And I haven't had a panic attack in well over a year now. I hope all of you who with struggle with anxiety, panic, intrusive thoughts, etc. can end up in a similar place one day.

Everything feels overwhelming at the moment. I recently transitioned into a corporate role as a math enrichment teacher after years of private tutoring where I taught a maximum of two students at a time. I feel significantly underpaid for my current workload, especially since I discovered I earn less than colleagues who have fewer students than I do.

I only have three hours to prepare for the entire day (which includes printing worksheets, grading, and lesson planning) and I am struggling to keep up with my growing roster. I find it impossible to provide individual attention when multiple students are in a session, and I often feel lost the moment class begins.

I haven’t seen the whole video but I am about to share something crucial about me that no one believed me at first on.
2 years ago, when I was still in school, I had suddenly started to feel stressed. That was the first warning sign.
Because within 3-4 months, my depression faded, eventually disappearing entirely by 11 months.
I thought I was going crazy. But it didn’t stop. I went to therapy while my body slowly caved in.
It’s been 2 years with no resolve.
College failed within 2 months. All I remember is toxicity, gaslighting, coercion and the specific words “You are not the exception” and “I don’t know is not an answer”. And I now am in full overdrive. In fact, so far into overdrive that I can’t tell if I am panicked anymore or not.
It has affected my weight, my sleep, my metabolism, everything.
And somehow I am spiteful enough to keep giving kindness out to the world.
It hurts.
It hurts so much.
But my 19 years of life can only be described as painful for me.
At 12 I feared I would be alone now, and I was right.
At 3, before I was adopted, I feared no one wanted me.
From 3-11 years old, I suffered from chronic nightmares, weekly for 8 years straight, so much so that at 7 years old, I was already developing advanced coping mechanisms.
And through it I was ostracized, bullied, backstabbed, rejected, downplayed, discouraged, disillusioned, and regularly confused.
Denied acceptance and offered rejection all the time. From special education misleading me to basic human decency denied for a some kind of reason.
My entire life could be explained like a constant form of reality just out of reach because I depended on my daydreams for the support I didn’t have. The love I didn’t get. The normalization of humanity the world refused to normalize for me.
And now, it’s gotten so bad that i actually just months ago had to quit therapy, because even there it infiltrated my mental system.
I found this channel at 14.
But despite all its taught me, the one thing that eludes me is the ability to feel relief.
I don’t know what normal feels like.
Socially.
Mentally.
Psychologically.
Physiologically.
Familiarly.
Existentially.
All of it.
And I still keep holding onto kindness, because it’s the very least I can do.
Because I don’t want anyone to ever feel what I feel.
That’s all.

A couple years ago, I had to look up the differences between apathy and enlightenment because I was worried I was going dead inside again (despite working so hard on developing emotional intelligence). Painful things that used to cause me to implode for months on end weren't hitting me like that anymore, and it scared me. It wasn't that the amount of pain was the same and I was just better at managing it. Those things legitimately hurt less from the start.

Do you want to know what the difference is between apathy and enlightenment? Because they feel remarkably similar in a lot of ways. 

Apathy puts you in a position where you feel very little, or nothing at all. Even the good things. But if the pain is easier just because you've aligned yourself with reality, you're still able to feel joy and passion at full volume. 

I still cry. I laugh every single day. I have pangs of empathy when I see an injured animal or a scared child. It's not gone, it's just... Different.

So if you're also in a position where you're healing from something that haunts you, this could be a good guideline for you. Regularly remind yourself of those differences, and then self-assess to see which one is a more accurate description for you at that time. Goals are easier to hit when you know they're there, when you can see the brass ring you're trying to grab.

comment_text: When it comes up in conversation, I tell people that I’m an ambivert. I can be super social and crave that sense of spontaneous energy and fun. But I also know that I need to be by myself to rest and recharge. I’m in my room, just watching videos or playing some games. The crappy part is when you have ADHD and you get stuck in this loop of being alone and you don’t want to do anything or see anyone. Texts get overlooked, no calls or FaceTime, and no interaction with anyone on social media (this is a big one for me). And it’s not like I’m doing it out of spite, but sometimes just the thought of stepping out and running into my roommates makes me feel guilty for not saying or doing anything with them. Our brains work differently so these episodes of staying in your room all day and not doing anything, but in your head you still need to get up and do the things you need to do… it gets really tiring. And then, of course, in most cases when I do leave my room, it ends up being okay and then I feel good about getting up. All of this to say having ADHD definitely can make this type of behavior worse, I understand it completely, but there’s also a light at the end of the tunnel and it’s okay to tell yourself that you’re doing the best you can, and you have control 🫶🏼

In my case, it's not so much hating or being overwhelmed in crowds. I always prefer a quiet place than a crowded one. If two friends invite me to go out and one of them goes with 10 people more and the other just two, I will definitely choose the latter. 
But my fear goes another way. I am scared if being judged. Since I was little, I was constantly thinking about what the others say or might say about me, and I still do at my 40's. So when I am in a crowd, like a wedding, I can't help but think that some people might be judging me. 
But this changes in some cases. If I go to some event and I am surrounded by people who are like me in some way, I feel confident that no one will say anything, and I feel totally comfortable. I have gone to many manga/otaku conventions, and every year I go to the Antwerp pride here in Belgium, and in both cases it's very crowded, and I always feel good. Why? Because I know everyone around me is like me and we share something, either being otakus or manga/anime fans or being part of the LGBT community. I know no one is judged in those events, and that gives me security. 
In the previous example of a wedding, they all are very different, and I don't know if we share anything or not.

comment_text: I recently volunteered at an event not knowing what I am doing as someone with an social anxiety caused by an anxiety disorder and it was really hard. I picked the last day at the latest shift to volunteer and that choice was very intentional. It meant I only had an hour to figure out everything and talk to crowds and can spend the rest of it helping to clean up and talking with the organizers one on one rather than a big crowd and reflecting on the experience. It took a lot of work to be able to get this far though and I purposely had to put myself into a situation that felt like hell for an hour so that next time it can be a little easier. Point is, I would not have done something like this a few years ago and would have probably started crying due to being overwhelmed and left, but it gets easier the more you challenge yourself and realise that people also have compassion. Counselling has also helped me a lot so I don't want to pretend I got this far alone, but I was really proud of myself and the organisers were really kind to me when I explained my anxiety to them which helped a lot when we got to talk one on one when they gave me pointers of things I can improve on and said I did an overall good job. Some people were not as understanding/knowledgeable on anxiety, telling me to "just relax", but I knew it was not out of malice and with practice it will improve.

OK (/ˌoʊˈkeɪ/ ⓘ), with spelling variations including okay, O.K. and many others, is an English word (originating in American English) denoting approval, acceptance, agreement, assent, acknowledgment, or a sign of indifference. OK is frequently used as a loanword in other languages. It has been described as the most frequently spoken or written word on the planet.[1]

"A round push button with the letters O and K as labels.
An OK button on a remote control
The origin of OK is disputed; however, most modern reference works hold that it originated around Boston as part of a fad in the late 1830s of abbreviating misspellings – that it is an initialism of "oll korrect" as a misspelling of "all correct". This origin was first described by linguist Allen Walker Read in the 1960s.

As an adjective, OK principally means "adequate" or "acceptable" as a contrast to "bad" ("The boss approved this, so it is OK to send out"); it can also mean "mediocre" when used in contrast with "good" ("The french fries were great, but the burger was just OK"). It fulfills a similar role as an adverb ("Wow, you did OK for your first time skiing!"). As an interjection, it can denote compliance ("OK, I will do that"),[2] or agreement ("OK, that is fine"). It can mean "assent" when it is used as a noun ("the boss gave her the OK to the purchase") or, more colloquially, as a verb ("the boss OKed the purchase"). OK, as an adjective, can express acknowledgement without approval.[3] As a versatile discourse marker or continuer, it can also be used with appropriate intonation to show doubt or to seek confirmation ("OK?", "Is that OK?").[4][2] Some of this variation in use and shape of the word is also found in other languages.[5]

I was going through a lot in my life the past 8+ months. A breakup, a traumatizing move, an awful flu bug middle of moving, lots of problems related to the move, health problems, family problems and then mental health problems from it all. I was drowning and very depressed.
At the same time, a new friend was going through similar things. Issues with her bf she almost broke up with him for, a move, a flu bug. 
Despite my problems, I was there to support her. I pushed her to communicate with him to work things out. I was there to listen to everything and try to help how I could. Meanwhile I was struggling to get up everyday.
Her life got better, mine did not. She's engaged. While she still has problems, all the major problems have passed. Some problems left are minor and can be worked out, or just part of daily life.
She told me one day that she couldn't hear about people's problems anymore because she needed to recharge her battery after everything. She worded it in a way that sounded directed at me, though I did know another friend of hers was having a rough time too. Considering everything with me, and what I did for her without question, that really stung and affected my trust in people. I get needing time, but it was worded like she viewed me as a problem she needed to get rid of. 
After when we would talk, she asked me a question as if to get a conversation going, I'd answer, being willing to open up a little, and she'd ignore it, time and again. She told me I was wrong about something I knew for a fact I was right about, could be easily searched up. Not just told, but worded it like I was an idiot and almost gaslighting me.
I've felt used and stupid for even trying honestly. I was there to help without question, even when I was at one of my worst points, but I can't have the same, even if only just to have someone there at all.
I've told all friends that I won't message them unless they message me first, not cutting off contact if needed or wanted, I need the time to heal and so much of what they'd talk about to me would hurt me.
One went off at me about me still speaking to my ex, how stupid that is, even though she did the same thing. She told me everyone rolls their eyes at me. Who says something like that?
My ex is 1 of 4 people I still speak to. 1 of 4 people who cares enough to check on me and still act like a friend should and respect my boundaries. Our breakup had nothing to do with not loving each other or anything bad happening, but a change in circumstances. He handled it poorly, but he was struggling a lot too. 

I bet down the road, these same friends I haven't heard from in weeks and explained the situation, will be upset with me for not reaching out to them. Will believe I don't care about them anymore. But whatever. The real ones understand. If any of them ever say anything, I'll let them know I was in an awful place, and those who cared and respected that still reached out to be there in the capacity I needed, which a lot of the time was simply asking how I am, not telling me all their problems and not caring about me, or wanting to do something with me that required no speaking of issues. Just watching or playing something we both enjoy. Thanks to them I'm better than I was. I'm lonely most of the time since it's not often I hear from them, but I'm better.
Being a good friend means doing what's within your capacity for them when they need it, not blaming them when you did too much. Not treating them poorly because of how you personally feel. Not guilting them. Not ignoring them. Not using them when you need someone and walking away when you don't. Not judging and laughing at them for making a decision that only affects their life.
